analogy.p: Imagine a jar of 100 marbles: 78 are blue (nitrogen), 21 are red (oxygen) and just one is a mix of green, yellow and clear marbles (argon, carbon dioxide and the rest). If you took out all the red marbles, as the hot copper does, you would see the number in the jar drop from 100 to 79. The analogy breaks down because real gas molecules are constantly moving and spread out with lots of space between them, and the composition is kept stable by natural cycles rather than someone refilling the jar.
analogy.t: Air as a jar of 100 marbles

bullets: The atmosphere is the layer of gases held around the Earth by gravity.
Dry air is roughly 4/5 nitrogen and 1/5 oxygen; everything else together is only about 1%.
The 'other gases' named by AQA are carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases (such as argon).
The proportions have been broadly stable for about 200 million years.
You may be asked to give a value as a fraction, a percentage or a ratio, so know all three forms.
This point links forwards to greenhouse gases (4.9.3), carbon footprint (4.9.4) and atmospheric pollutants (4.9.5).
core.p: AQA 4.9.2 asks you to know the **composition of the atmosphere today** and that the proportions of the different gases have been **much the same for the past 200 million years**. You need to say that about **four-fifths (approximately 80%) is nitrogen**, about **one-fifth (approximately 20%) is oxygen**, and that there are **small proportions of various other gases**, including **carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases**. You also need to use and interpret percentage and volume data about air, which is why this topic shows up in calculation questions as well as recall questions.

bullets: **Nitrogen (N2): about 78%**, so roughly four-fifths.
**Oxygen (O2): about 21%**, so roughly one-fifth.
**Argon (Ar): about 0.9%**, the most common noble gas in air.
**Carbon dioxide (CO2): about 0.04%**, a trace gas but very important for climate and photosynthesis.
**Water vapour (H2O):** varies from almost 0% to about 4% depending on weather and location, which is why the figures are given for dry air.
Other noble gases (neon, helium, krypton, xenon) are present in tiny traces.
78 + 21 + 0.9 + 0.04 is about 99.9%, and the last bits are the other trace gases, so the total is 100%.
core.h: The composition of dry air (the numbers to learn)
core.p: The percentages below are for **dry air**, which means air with the variable amount of water vapour left out. Nitrogen makes up **78%** by volume and oxygen **21%**, so together they account for 99% of the air. The remaining **1%** is mostly argon (about 0.93%) with a tiny amount of carbon dioxide (about 0.04%) and traces of neon, helium, krypton, xenon and others. For exam answers, 'about 80% nitrogen and about 20% oxygen' is the safest wording because it is exactly what the specification says, and more precise values are accepted when they are correct.

bullets: Nitrogen is a colourless, odourless gas that is slightly less dense than air.
The strong N≡N triple bond explains why it is unreactive and so stays in the atmosphere.
It is used industrially to make ammonia (Haber process) and so fertilisers.
Nitrogen is also used to create an inert atmosphere, for example in food packaging to stop food reacting with oxygen.
Nitrogen oxides only form at very high temperatures, for example in car engines or lightning, where N2 and O2 react.
Link: nitrogen is a reactant in the Haber process, covered later in 4.10.
core.p: Nitrogen is the main gas in the air because it is **very unreactive**. The two nitrogen atoms in an N2 molecule are joined by a **triple covalent bond**, which is very strong and needs a lot of energy to break. Because of this, nitrogen does not react with most substances at ordinary temperatures, so it has built up in the atmosphere and has not been used up by chemical reactions. Nitrogen is only converted into compounds by lightning, by nitrogen-fixing bacteria, and by industrial processes such as the Haber process.

bullets: Oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration in living things.
Oxygen is needed for combustion; fuels burn faster in pure oxygen than in air because air is only 21% oxygen.
Oxygen reacts with metals to form oxides (oxidation), for example iron rusting needs oxygen and water.
The build-up of oxygen is explained by photosynthesis (see 4.9.1 Evolution of the atmosphere).
The test for oxygen is that it relights a glowing splint.
Oxygen can be separated from air by fractional distillation of liquid air, used in steelmaking and hospitals.
core.p: About one-fifth of the air is oxygen, and this is the gas that makes **combustion, respiration and rusting** possible. Oxygen is present in this amount today because of **photosynthesis**: plants and algae took in carbon dioxide and released oxygen over billions of years, which built up the level from almost none in the early atmosphere. The level has stayed near 21% because oxygen used in respiration and burning is balanced by oxygen produced in photosynthesis. Oxygen is also the reactant removed from air in the copper experiment in this note.

bullets: Carbon dioxide is about 0.04% (roughly 420 parts per million today).
Carbon dioxide is used by plants in photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen.
Water vapour varies between nearly 0% and about 4%, which is why 'dry air' values are quoted.
Both gases are greenhouse gases (see the next note, 4.9.3).
The level of carbon dioxide is rising because of human activities such as burning fossil fuels.
Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky; this is the test for carbon dioxide.
core.h: Carbon dioxide and water vapour: small amounts, big effects
core.p: Carbon dioxide makes up only about **0.04%** of the atmosphere, yet it has a major effect on the climate because it is a **greenhouse gas**. Water vapour is also a greenhouse gas, but its amount in the air changes a lot from place to place and day to day. Both are involved in cycles: carbon dioxide is removed by photosynthesis and dissolving in the oceans, and returned by respiration, combustion and decay; water vapour is added by evaporation and removed by condensation and rain. Because their quantities can change, these two are the gases whose levels matter most for global warming.

bullets: Argon is about 0.93% of dry air and is the third most abundant gas.
Noble gases exist as single atoms (monatomic), not molecules.
They are unreactive because of their full outer shell (stable electron arrangement).
Argon is used in filament lamps to stop the hot filament reacting with oxygen, and in welding to protect hot metal.
Helium is used in balloons and airships because it is less dense than air and non-flammable.
Neon is used in advertising signs because it glows red-orange when electricity passes through it.
Link: the noble gases are covered in 4.1 and 4.2 (Group 0 trends).
core.h: The noble gases in the air
core.p: The noble gases (Group 0) are **argon, neon, helium, krypton and xenon**, and they make up under 1% of the air, mostly argon. They are very **unreactive** because their atoms have full outer shells of electrons, so they do not need to gain, lose or share electrons. This is why they have stayed in the atmosphere in a constant proportion. Argon is used where an inert atmosphere is needed, such as in filament lamps and in welding.

bullets: The balance is maintained by natural cycles, mainly the carbon cycle and the oxygen cycle.
Photosynthesis and respiration are roughly balanced over long periods.
Nitrogen's low reactivity means it is barely removed, so it stays near 78%.
The early atmosphere (billions of years ago) was mostly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen; this changed over time.
The only big recent change is the rise in carbon dioxide caused by human activity, from about 0.028% to about 0.042%.
Even a small change in carbon dioxide matters because it is a greenhouse gas.
core.h: Why the proportions have stayed the same for 200 million years
core.p: The specification says the proportions of the gases have been **much the same for the past 200 million years**. This does not mean nothing changes; it means that processes adding a gas and processes removing it are in balance. For example, photosynthesis adds oxygen and removes carbon dioxide, while respiration, combustion and decay remove oxygen and add carbon dioxide. Nitrogen is so unreactive that very little is removed. The key point is that the early atmosphere was very different (4.9.1), but the modern composition settled down and remained stable long before humans appeared.

bullets: Start with 100 cm3 of air in one syringe, connected through a tube of heated copper to an empty second syringe.
Heat the copper strongly and push the air slowly from one syringe to the other several times.
Copper turns from shiny brown to black copper oxide as it reacts with oxygen.
Stop heating and **let the apparatus cool back to room temperature** before reading the final volume, because hot gas takes up more volume.
Percentage of oxygen = (decrease in volume ÷ starting volume) × 100.
The final volume is about 79 cm3, so the decrease is about 21 cm3, which gives about 21% oxygen.
Use excess copper so that there is enough to react with all the oxygen; the copper should not all turn black.
Repeating the experiment and calculating a mean improves reliability.
core.h: How to find the percentage of oxygen in air (copper experiment)
core.p: A classic experiment measures the proportion of oxygen by **removing it from a fixed volume of air** and seeing how much the volume falls. Excess copper is heated in a sealed system of two gas syringes, and the air is pushed backwards and forwards over the hot copper so that all the oxygen reacts. The equation is **2Cu + O2 → 2CuO**. Only the oxygen is used up, because nitrogen and the noble gases do not react with hot copper, so the loss in volume equals the volume of oxygen that was in the air.

bullets: Fractions: four-fifths = 80%, one-fifth = 20%; so 'about 4:1' is the nitrogen to oxygen ratio.
Volume of oxygen in 500 cm3 of air = 21 ÷ 100 × 500 = 105 cm3.
Volume of nitrogen in 2.0 dm3 of air = 78 ÷ 100 × 2.0 = 1.56 dm3.
To find the percentage from volumes: (part ÷ whole) × 100.
The percentages of all gases in dry air must add up to 100%; a missing value is 100 minus the sum of the others.
In ppm questions, 1% = 10 000 ppm, so 0.04% = 400 ppm.
Check that your answer is sensible: oxygen should be about one-fifth of the air.
core.h: Using composition data: calculating volumes of gases
core.p: Exam questions often give a volume of air and ask for the volume of a particular gas, or give percentages in a table and ask you to complete or interpret it. The method is simple: **volume of gas = (percentage ÷ 100) × total volume of air**. Always include units (cm3, dm3 or m3) and make sure percentages add up to 100%. If you are given a pie chart or bar chart, read the proportion carefully; a bar showing 78% should be a little under four-fifths of the whole bar.

bullets: On a pie chart, nitrogen takes up about 281° (78% × 3.6) and oxygen about 76° (21% × 3.6).
Always use the scale: read values from the axis, do not guess.
Describe a graph with 'from ... to ... between ... and ...' using actual numbers.
For a flat line over 200 million years, say the proportion is 'constant' or 'stable' and quote the value.
Correlation does not prove cause: two things changing together does not prove one causes the other.
Convert between ppm and % when comparing data sets: divide ppm by 10 000 for %.
core.p: You may be given a pie chart, bar chart or table of atmospheric composition, or a graph showing how a gas level has changed over time. For a pie chart, the angle is proportional to the percentage (360° = 100%, so 1% = 3.6°). For a graph, describe the **trend** (increasing, decreasing or constant), quote **figures with units** from the graph, and say whether the rise is steady or speeding up. Remember that a tiny percentage cannot be seen on a pie chart, so trace gases are often grouped as 'other'.

bullets: Link to 4.9.1: oxygen and nitrogen increased and carbon dioxide decreased over billions of years.
Link to 4.9.3: carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour are greenhouse gases.
Link to 4.9.5: carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and particulates are pollutants from burning fuels.
Link to 4.10: nitrogen from the air is the source of nitrogen in ammonia and fertilisers.
Link to 4.7 (rates): increased oxygen concentration increases the rate of combustion.
Higher-tier style reasoning: nitrogen is abundant because it is unreactive; oxygen is abundant because of photosynthesis.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher tier ideas
core.p: This point sets up the whole of the atmosphere topic. The **evolution of the atmosphere** explains how the present composition came about, the **greenhouse gases** point explains why tiny amounts of carbon dioxide and methane matter, and the **atmospheric pollutants** point covers gases such as carbon monoxide and sulfur dioxide that are not normally part of dry air in large amounts. The composition of air also matters for combustion calculations and for the Haber process, which uses nitrogen from the air. At Higher tier you may be asked to explain data rather than simply state it, so always link the property of the gas to why it is present in that amount.

bullets: A candle burning in a closed jar goes out when the oxygen is used, leaving mostly nitrogen and carbon dioxide.
Rusting of iron in a closed tube uses up about one-fifth of the air, as with the copper experiment.
At altitude the percentage of oxygen is still about 21%, but the pressure is lower so there is less oxygen per breath.
Exhaled air contains less oxygen (about 16%) and more carbon dioxide (about 4%) than inhaled air.
Nitrogen packaging 'flushes' out oxygen to slow down the oxidation of food.
Liquid air can be fractionally distilled to separate nitrogen, oxygen and argon because they have different boiling points.
core.p: Examiners like to set this topic in new contexts, so be ready to apply your knowledge. A mountaineer breathes air that has the same percentage of oxygen at altitude, but the air is thinner so there are fewer oxygen molecules per breath. A candle in a sealed jar goes out when the oxygen is used up even though most of the air (nitrogen) remains. Food packed in nitrogen or argon stays fresh longer because there is no oxygen to react with. In each case the idea is the same: the **proportion** of each gas matters, and the unreactive gases are the ones that stay behind.

exam: 'State' or 'give' (1 mark): write the fact only, for example 'about 78% nitrogen' or 'about four-fifths nitrogen'. Include the number or fraction when asked for the proportion.
'Name two gases found in small amounts in the air' (2 marks): carbon dioxide, argon, water vapour, other noble gases. Avoid naming nitrogen or oxygen if the question says 'small amounts'.

'Describe the composition of the atmosphere today' (2-3 marks): mention about four-fifths nitrogen, about one-fifth oxygen, and small amounts of other gases such as carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases.

Calculation questions (2 marks): method mark for percentage ÷ 100 × total volume, answer mark for correct value with units; show your working because a correct method gains a mark even if the arithmetic is wrong.
Percentage-from-experiment questions (2-3 marks): use (starting volume − final volume) ÷ starting volume × 100. State the fall in volume first.
Practical evaluation (3-4 marks): say why the apparatus must cool, why excess copper is used, why the gas is passed back and forth, and how to improve reliability by repeating and finding a mean.
'Explain why nitrogen is unreactive' (2 marks): strong triple covalent bond; a lot of energy is needed to break it.
'Explain why the proportion of oxygen has stayed the same' (3 marks): photosynthesis produces oxygen; respiration and combustion use oxygen; the processes balance.
Pie chart and graph questions: use values from the chart, give units, and state the trend with numbers; for a pie chart, convert angles with angle ÷ 360 × 100.
Be careful with 'dry air': if water vapour is mentioned, say its amount varies, and that is why the percentage in dry air is used.
Use the board's wording: 'approximately four-fifths', 'approximately one-fifth' and 'small proportions of various other gases'.

mistakes.r: Air is about 78% nitrogen and about 21% oxygen; nitrogen is the most abundant gas.
mistakes.w: Air is 100% oxygen / air is mostly oxygen.

mistakes.r: Air is a mixture of mainly nitrogen and oxygen, with small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide, water vapour and other noble gases.
mistakes.w: Air is made of oxygen and carbon dioxide only.

mistakes.r: Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04% of the atmosphere, but it is important because it is a greenhouse gas.
mistakes.w: Carbon dioxide makes up a large part of the air.

mistakes.r: Nitrogen is unreactive because of the very strong triple covalent bond between its atoms; it is not in Group 0.
mistakes.w: Nitrogen is unreactive because it is a noble gas.

mistakes.r: Copper reacts with the oxygen in the air to form copper oxide; only the oxygen is removed.
mistakes.w: The copper in the experiment 'absorbs' the air.

mistakes.r: Allow the apparatus to cool to room temperature before reading the final volume, otherwise the gas is expanded and the result is too low.
mistakes.w: Reading the syringe volume while it is still hot.

mistakes.r: The proportions have been much the same for the last 200 million years.
mistakes.w: The percentage of oxygen has changed a lot in the last 200 million years.

mistakes.r: The amount of water vapour varies, which is why composition is quoted for dry air.
mistakes.w: Percentages of water vapour are fixed.

summary: Know that the atmosphere today is about four-fifths (78%) nitrogen and one-fifth (21%) oxygen, with small proportions of carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases such as argon, and that this has been much the same for 200 million years. You must be able to use and interpret percentage data, calculate volumes of gases in air and explain the oxygen-in-air experiment. It matters because it underpins the greenhouse gas, pollution and resource topics.

terms.d: The layer of gases surrounding the Earth, held in place by gravity.
Air with the water vapour removed, used so that the percentages of the other gases are constant.
The most abundant gas in the air at about 78% (approximately four-fifths); it is unreactive.
The second most abundant gas in the air at about 21% (approximately one-fifth); it is needed for respiration and combustion.
A noble gas making up about 0.9% of the air; it is unreactive.
A trace gas making up about 0.04% of the air; it is a greenhouse gas and is used in photosynthesis.
Water as a gas in the air; the amount varies with weather and location, and it is a greenhouse gas.
The unreactive Group 0 elements (helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon) with full outer shells; found in very small amounts in the air.
The fraction or percentage of the total made up by one component, such as one-fifth of air being oxygen.
The volume of a gas divided by the total volume of the mixture, multiplied by 100.
Does not easily take part in chemical reactions; applies to nitrogen (strong triple bond) and noble gases (full outer shell).
The process in which plants and algae use carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen, using light energy.
The process that releases energy from glucose in living things, using oxygen and producing carbon dioxide and water.
A gas in the atmosphere that absorbs infrared radiation from the Earth; carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour are examples.
A unit of concentration: 1 part in 1 000 000, so 10 000 ppm = 1%.
Two or more substances that are not chemically joined, so air is a mixture of gases and can be separated by physical methods.

worked.q: A laboratory has 250 dm3 of dry air. Calculate the volume of oxygen and the volume of nitrogen in it, using 21% oxygen and 78% nitrogen. (3 marks)
steps: Volume of gas = percentage ÷ 100 × total volume.
Check: the two add up to 247.5 dm3, leaving 2.5 dm3 for the 1% of other gases, which matches 1% of 250.

worked.ans: (a) 21%; (b) 2Cu + O2 → 2CuO; (c) hot gas expands so the final volume reads too high, so the oxygen percentage reads too low.
worked.q: 100 cm3 of air is passed over hot excess copper until no further change occurs. The apparatus is cooled and the final volume is 79 cm3. (a) Calculate the percentage of oxygen in the air. (b) Write the equation for the reaction. (c) Give a reason why the result may be too low. (4 marks)
steps: Decrease in volume = 100 − 79 = 21 cm3, which is the oxygen used.

If the apparatus was not cooled, the gas is warmer and takes up more volume, so the decrease appears smaller; also, if not all oxygen reacted (not enough copper or not enough heating) the decrease is too small.

worked.ans: The atmosphere is about 78% (approximately four-fifths) nitrogen and about 21% (approximately one-fifth) oxygen, with small proportions of other gases such as argon and other noble gases, carbon dioxide and water vapour. Nitrogen is the most abundant because it is unreactive: the two atoms in a nitrogen molecule are joined by a strong triple covalent bond that needs a lot of energy to break, so nitrogen is not used up in reactions and remains in the atmosphere.
worked.q: Describe the composition of the Earth's atmosphere today and explain why the proportion of nitrogen is so high. (4 marks)
steps: State the composition: about four-fifths (78%) nitrogen and about one-fifth (21%) oxygen.
Mention the small proportions of other gases: argon and other noble gases, carbon dioxide (about 0.04%) and water vapour.
Explain nitrogen: it is unreactive because of the strong triple covalent bond between its atoms.
So it is not used up in reactions and has built up in the atmosphere.
